name: The Plains of Concepts
description: Foundational networking theory. Everything else builds on this.

nodes.name: The Seven Layers
nodes.description: The OSI Model — Layer 1 through Layer 7.

encounters.question: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets across different networks using IP addresses?
encounters.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing (IP) and routing. Layer 2 uses MAC addresses, Layer 4 handles TCP/UDP, Layer 5 manages sessions.

encounters.question: Which OSI layer handles MAC addressing and frames?
encounters.explanation: Layer 2 (Data Link) uses MAC addresses for local delivery and encapsulates data into frames. It includes Ethernet and 802.11 Wi-Fi.

encounters.question: TCP and UDP operate at which OSI layer?
encounters.explanation: Layer 4 (Transport) provides end-to-end communication. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and faster.

encounters.question: What is the correct order of OSI layers from Layer 1 to Layer 7?
options: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Physical, Network, Data Link, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Physical, Data Link, Transport, Network, Session, Presentation, Application
Physical, Data Link, Network, Session, Transport, Presentation, Application
encounters.explanation: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

encounters.question: Which layer converts data between formats, handles encryption, and compression?
encounters.explanation: Layer 6 (Presentation) translates, encrypts, and compresses data for the Application layer. TLS/SSL operates here.

encounters.question: What PDU (Protocol Data Unit) is used at Layer 4 (Transport)?
encounters.explanation: Layer 4 PDU is a Segment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP). Layer 3 = Packet, Layer 2 = Frame, Layer 1 = Bit.

encounters.question: Which OSI layer establishes, manages, and terminates communication sessions?
encounters.explanation: Layer 5 (Session) manages dialogue control and synchronization between applications. NetBIOS and RPC operate at this layer.

encounters.question: A switch operates at Layer 2. What table does it use to forward frames?
encounters.explanation: Switches build and maintain a MAC address table (Content Addressable Memory) mapping MAC addresses to port numbers for intelligent frame forwarding.

encounters.question: HTTP, FTP, and DNS operate at which OSI layer?
encounters.explanation: Layer 7 (Application) is the layer end-user protocols interact with directly — HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP, SNMP all live here.

encounters.question: During encapsulation, which layer adds a source and destination IP address to the PDU?
encounters.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) adds the IP header containing source and destination IP addresses, creating a packet from the Layer 4 segment.

nodes.name: The Toolbox
nodes.description: Networking appliances — routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers, proxies.

encounters.question: A hub differs from a switch in that a hub:
options: Makes intelligent forwarding decisions based on MAC addresses
Broadcasts all traffic out all ports, creating one large collision domain
Operates at Layer 3 and routes between networks
Filters traffic based on security policies
encounters.explanation: Hubs operate at Layer 1 and repeat all traffic out every port. Switches use MAC tables to forward only to the correct port, reducing collisions.

encounters.question: What is the primary function of a load balancer?
options: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent overload
Assigns IP addresses to clients on a network
Monitors network traffic for intrusion attempts
encounters.explanation: Load balancers distribute client requests across a server pool, improving availability and preventing any single server from being overwhelmed.

encounters.question: What is the key difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: IDS encrypts traffic; IPS decrypts traffic
IDS detects and alerts; IPS detects AND actively blocks threats
IDS is hardware-only; IPS is software-only
IDS operates at Layer 7; IPS at Layer 3
encounters.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) monitors AND blocks/prevents threats inline in the traffic path.

encounters.question: A proxy server sits between clients and the internet. What does it primarily provide?
options: Caching, content filtering, and anonymity for clients
encounters.explanation: Proxy servers cache web content, filter URLs/content, and can anonymize client IP addresses. Forward proxies serve clients; reverse proxies serve servers.

encounters.question: What device connects networks using different media types (e.g., copper to fiber)?
encounters.explanation: Media converters translate between different physical media types, such as copper UTP to fiber optic, operating at Layer 1.

encounters.question: What is a UTM (Unified Threat Management) device?
options: A high-speed router for ISP core networks
An all-in-one security appliance combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, and content filtering
A wireless controller managing multiple access points
A load balancer with SSL offloading capability
encounters.explanation: UTM devices consolidate multiple security functions (firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, web filter, VPN) into a single appliance, simplifying security management.

encounters.question: A Layer 3 switch differs from a Layer 2 switch because it can:
options: Route between VLANs without a separate router
Handle only 1000 Mbps or higher speeds
encounters.explanation: Layer 3 switches have routing capabilities built in, allowing inter-VLAN routing without a dedicated router. They combine switching speed with routing intelligence.

encounters.question: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless packet filter in that it:
options: Blocks all traffic by default and requires explicit allow rules
Tracks the state of active TCP connections and validates returning traffic
Only inspects source and destination IP addresses
encounters.explanation: Stateful firewalls maintain a connection state table, allowing return traffic for established sessions. Stateless filters check each packet independently without context.

encounters.question: What network device regenerates a signal to extend cable distance beyond its normal limit?
encounters.explanation: Repeaters operate at Layer 1 and boost/regenerate signals to extend cable reach. Modern switches effectively include this functionality per-port.

encounters.question: An administrator needs to inspect and filter traffic at Layer 7 (application level) including HTTPS content. What device is needed?
options: IDS sensor in passive tap mode
encounters.explanation: NGFWs can perform SSL/TLS decryption and application-level (Layer 7) inspection. Standard firewalls cannot inspect encrypted HTTPS payloads without SSL offloading.

nodes.name: The Cloud
nodes.description: Cloud computing — NFV, VPC, service models (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS), deployment models.

encounters.question: Which cloud service model provides virtual machines, storage, and raw networking infrastructure?
encounters.explanation: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) provides raw compute, storage, and networking. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine.

encounters.question: Microsoft Office 365 and Gmail are examples of which cloud service model?
encounters.explanation: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers fully managed applications over the internet. The provider manages everything — infrastructure, platform, and software.

encounters.question: AWS Elastic Beanstalk and Google App Engine are examples of which cloud service model?
encounters.explanation: PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides a managed runtime environment for developers to deploy applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.

encounters.question: What is NFV (Network Functions Virtualization)?
options: A method of assigning virtual IP addresses
Replacing dedicated physical network appliances with software running on commodity hardware
A protocol for encrypting virtual machine traffic
A type of cloud backup service
encounters.explanation: NFV decouples network functions (firewalls, routers, load balancers) from proprietary hardware, running them as virtual machines on standard servers.

encounters.question: What is a VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)?
options: A VPN protocol for site-to-site connectivity
An isolated, logically partitioned section of a public cloud provider's infrastructure
A virtual private switch in an on-premises data center
A type of cloud storage with private encryption keys
encounters.explanation: A VPC (e.g., AWS VPC, Azure VNet) gives organizations a private, isolated network segment within a public cloud, with control over IP ranges, subnets, and routing.

encounters.question: A hybrid cloud is characterized by:
options: Multiple public cloud providers used simultaneously (multi-cloud)
A mix of private and public cloud with data and applications shared between them
Cloud infrastructure owned exclusively by one organization
encounters.explanation: Hybrid cloud combines private cloud (on-premises) with public cloud, allowing workloads to move between them based on cost, compliance, or capacity needs.

encounters.question: What cloud characteristic describes the ability to automatically scale resources up or down based on demand?
encounters.explanation: Rapid elasticity (one of NIST's 5 cloud characteristics) means resources can scale out/in quickly and automatically, appearing unlimited to the consumer.

encounters.question: Multi-tenancy in cloud computing means:
options: A single organization using multiple cloud providers
Multiple customers sharing the same physical infrastructure while remaining logically isolated
Multiple applications running on the same virtual machine
Cloud resources distributed across multiple geographic regions
encounters.explanation: Multi-tenancy is a core cloud principle: shared physical resources serve multiple customers (tenants) with logical isolation via virtualization and access controls.

encounters.question: Which cloud deployment model offers an organization the MOST control and security?
encounters.explanation: Private cloud runs on dedicated infrastructure (on-premises or hosted), giving full control over security, compliance, and customization — at higher cost.

encounters.question: A company needs cloud infrastructure shared with other organizations that have similar compliance requirements (e.g., HIPAA). Which deployment model fits?
encounters.explanation: Community cloud is shared infrastructure for organizations with common concerns (e.g., government agencies sharing FISMA requirements, or hospitals sharing HIPAA compliance).

nodes.name: The Secret Codes
nodes.description: Ports and protocols — know these cold for the exam.

encounters.question: What port does FTP use for its control channel?
encounters.explanation: FTP uses port 21 for the control channel (commands) and port 20 for the data channel (active mode). Both are unencrypted.

encounters.question: SSH uses which port?
encounters.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) uses port 22. It provides encrypted remote access and is the secure replacement for Telnet (port 23).

encounters.question: SMTP (email sending) uses which port?
encounters.explanation: SMTP uses port 25 for server-to-server email relay. Port 587 is used for client submission (SMTP with auth). Port 110 is POP3, port 143 is IMAP.

encounters.question: DNS uses which port?
encounters.explanation: DNS uses port 53. It typically uses UDP for queries and TCP for zone transfers and responses over 512 bytes.

encounters.question: HTTPS uses which port?
encounters.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS/SSL) uses port 443. HTTP uses port 80. HTTPS provides encryption, authentication, and data integrity.

encounters.question: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) uses which port?
encounters.explanation: RDP uses port 3389. It provides graphical remote access to Windows systems. VNC uses port 5900, SSH uses 22, Telnet uses 23.

encounters.question: DHCP server listens on which port?
encounters.explanation: DHCP server listens on UDP port 67; clients use UDP port 68. Clients broadcast DHCPDISCOVER since they have no IP yet.

encounters.question: SNMP uses which port?
encounters.explanation: SNMP uses UDP port 161 for agent polling (manager→agent) and UDP port 162 for traps (agent→manager notifications). Port 514 is Syslog.

encounters.question: A network admin needs to securely transfer files. Which protocol and port should they use?
encounters.explanation: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) runs over SSH on port 22, providing encrypted file transfer. SCP also uses port 22. TFTP (port 69) and FTP (port 21) are unencrypted.

encounters.question: Which combination of ports is associated with Syslog and LDAP respectively?
encounters.explanation: Syslog uses UDP port 514 (TCP 514/6514 for TLS). LDAP uses port 389 (unencrypted); LDAPS uses 636 (encrypted). Know both pairs for the exam.

nodes.name: The Physical Path
nodes.description: Network media — fiber optics, copper cabling, connectors, transceivers.

encounters.question: What connector type is standard for Cat5e and Cat6 UTP cables?
encounters.explanation: RJ-45 is the standard 8-pin connector for Ethernet (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a). RJ-11 is for telephone (6-pin). LC and SC are fiber connectors.

encounters.question: What is the main advantage of fiber optic cable over copper UTP?
options: Immune to electromagnetic interference (EMI) and supports much longer distances
Compatible with all RJ-45 interfaces without transceivers
encounters.explanation: Fiber uses light instead of electrical signals, making it immune to EMI/RFI and capable of runs exceeding 100km (single-mode). Copper is limited to 100m.

encounters.question: What is the maximum distance for Cat5e and Cat6 at 1 Gbps?
encounters.explanation: Both Cat5e and Cat6 support 1 Gbps at up to 100 meters (328 feet). Cat6 additionally supports 10 Gbps up to 55 meters.

encounters.question: Single-mode fiber (SMF) is characterized by:
options: LED light source, short distances up to 2km
Multiple light paths, used in data centers up to 550m
Single light path using laser, capable of very long distances (up to 100km+)
Yellow jacket cables used for outdoor installations only
encounters.explanation: SMF has a narrow 8-10 micron core and uses a laser light source with a single light path. It supports long-distance runs (tens to hundreds of km) used in WANs and service providers.

encounters.question: Which fiber connector is small form-factor and commonly used in data center patch panels?
encounters.explanation: LC (Lucent Connector) is a small form-factor connector used widely in data centers. ST uses a twist-lock mechanism (older), SC has a push-pull design, FC is for high-vibration environments.

encounters.question: Multi-mode fiber (MMF) supports what approximate maximum distance at 10 Gbps?
encounters.explanation: OM3 multi-mode fiber supports 10 Gbps up to 300m; OM4 up to 550m. Single-mode supports 10 Gbps over much longer distances (10km+).

encounters.question: What hot-swappable transceiver module is commonly used to connect fiber to a switch?
encounters.explanation: SFP (Small Form-factor Pluggable) handles 1 Gbps; SFP+ handles 10 Gbps. Both are hot-swappable and support various fiber and copper media via pluggable optics.

encounters.question: Cat6a supports 10 Gbps at what maximum distance?
encounters.explanation: Cat6a (Augmented Category 6) supports 10 Gbps at the full 100-meter run, unlike standard Cat6 which is limited to 55m at 10 Gbps.

encounters.question: What is a straight-through cable used for?
options: Connecting a PC directly to another PC
Connecting unlike devices such as a PC to a switch or switch to a router
Connecting a router to a DSL modem
encounters.explanation: Straight-through cables connect unlike devices (PC→switch, switch→router). Crossover cables connect like devices (switch→switch, PC→PC). Modern NICs support Auto-MDIX, making this less critical.

encounters.question: A technician needs to connect two buildings 400 meters apart at 10 Gbps. What is the best cable choice?
encounters.explanation: At 400 meters, copper is out (100m max). OM3 MMF supports only 300m at 10 Gbps. Only single-mode fiber supports 10 Gbps over 400m — and much further.

nodes.name: The Layout
nodes.description: Network topologies — mesh, star, spine-and-leaf, north-south vs east-west traffic.

encounters.question: In a star topology, what device serves as the central connection point?
encounters.explanation: Star topology connects all devices to a central hub or switch. Hub creates one collision domain; switch creates per-port collision domains.

encounters.question: What is the main weakness of a bus topology?
options: A break anywhere in the shared cable takes down the entire network
Highest cost topology due to redundant cabling
encounters.explanation: Bus topology uses a single shared backbone cable. Any break or fault in the bus kills connectivity for all devices — it has a single point of failure.

encounters.question: Which topology connects EVERY device to every other device, providing maximum redundancy?
encounters.explanation: Full mesh connects every node to every other node, eliminating single points of failure. Expensive (n*(n-1)/2 connections) but used in high-availability core networks.

encounters.question: Spine-and-leaf architecture is primarily designed for which environment?
options: Data centers with high east-west traffic
encounters.explanation: Spine-and-leaf provides equal-cost paths between any two leaf switches, minimizing latency for server-to-server (east-west) traffic in modern data centers.

encounters.question: What is 'north-south' traffic in a data center context?
options: Traffic between servers within the same data center
Traffic flowing between external clients and servers inside the data center
Traffic on the management network between servers
Traffic routed through the core layer to distribution
encounters.explanation: North-south traffic flows between the data center and external users/internet. East-west traffic flows between servers within the data center (which has grown dramatically with virtualization).

encounters.question: The traditional three-tier network architecture consists of which layers?
encounters.explanation: The three-tier model: Core (high-speed backbone), Distribution (policy/routing between access and core), Access (end-device connectivity). Still common in enterprise campus networks.

encounters.question: What is 'east-west' traffic and why has it become more important?
options: WAN traffic between regional offices — important for SD-WAN
Server-to-server traffic within a data center — grown dramatically due to virtualization and microservices
Traffic between subnets in the access layer
Wireless traffic between access points in different frequency bands
encounters.explanation: East-west traffic between servers/VMs now dominates data centers due to virtualization, microservices, and distributed applications. Spine-and-leaf is designed to handle it efficiently.

encounters.question: In a ring topology, what happens when one node or link fails?
options: Only the failed node is isolated; all others continue
The entire ring fails unless it supports dual-ring (counter-rotating) redundancy
Traffic is automatically rerouted through the star topology fallback
encounters.explanation: A single ring has one path; any break disrupts all communication. SONET/SDH uses dual counter-rotating rings for fault tolerance. STP is for Ethernet switched networks, not rings.

encounters.question: A 'collapsed core' design combines which two layers of the three-tier model?
encounters.explanation: Collapsed core merges the Core and Distribution layers into a single device/layer, common in small-medium networks where separate core switches are cost-prohibitive.

encounters.question: In spine-and-leaf architecture, every leaf switch connects to every spine switch. This provides:
options: A single path between any two servers — simple but limited
Equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing providing consistent, low-latency paths between any two leaf switches in exactly two hops
Layer 2 flooding across all leaf switches for broadcast domains
Automatic failover using Spanning Tree Protocol
encounters.explanation: Spine-and-leaf guarantees any-to-any communication in exactly two hops (leaf→spine→leaf), providing predictable latency and ECMP load sharing. STP is actively avoided in these designs.

nodes.name: The Address Book
nodes.description: IPv4 — classes, private ranges, subnetting, CIDR. Know this cold.

encounters.question: Which of the following is a private IPv4 address range?
What subnet mask corresponds to /24 in CIDR notation?
encounters.explanation: /24 means 24 bits are the network portion. In dotted-decimal: 255.255.255.0 (three octets of 255). This is the classic Class C subnet mask.

encounters.question: How many usable host addresses does a /24 subnet provide?
encounters.explanation: /24 has 256 total addresses (2^8). Subtract 1 for network address and 1 for broadcast = 254 usable hosts.

encounters.question: What is the IPv4 loopback address?
encounters.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address (also ::1 in IPv6). The entire 127.0.0.0/8 range is reserved for loopback. Used to test the TCP/IP stack on the local machine.

encounters.question: What is the APIPA address range used when a DHCP server is unreachable?
encounters.explanation: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) assigns addresses in the 169.254.0.0/16 range when a DHCP server is unavailable. A host with 169.254.x.x cannot communicate off its subnet.

encounters.question: What subnet mask corresponds to /26?
encounters.explanation: /26 has 26 network bits. The last octet has 2 host bits borrowed: 11000000 = 192. So: 255.255.255.192. Each /26 subnet has 64 addresses (62 usable).

encounters.question: How many usable hosts are in a /26 subnet?
encounters.explanation: /26 has 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 total addresses. Subtract network and broadcast = 62 usable hosts. Subnets per /24: 4 subnets of 64 addresses each.

encounters.question: What is the purpose of a default gateway?
options: Assigns IP addresses to hosts on a subnet
Routes traffic destined for addresses outside the local subnet
Translates private IP addresses to public IP addresses
Resolves domain names to IP addresses
encounters.explanation: The default gateway is the router interface on the local subnet. When a host needs to send traffic to a different network, it forwards the packet to the default gateway.

encounters.question: A /30 subnet is typically used for what purpose?
options: Server farms with hundreds of hosts
Point-to-point links between routers (2 usable hosts)
encounters.explanation: /30 has 2 host bits: 4 total addresses, 2 usable. Perfect for point-to-point router links where only two addresses are needed — one per end.

encounters.question: Host A has IP 192.168.10.75/27. What is its subnet address?
encounters.explanation: /27 = 32 hosts per subnet. Subnets: .0-.31, .32-.63, .64-.95, .96-.127... Host .75 falls in the .64-.95 range. Subnet address is 192.168.10.64/27.

nodes.name: The New Wave
nodes.description: SDN, SASE, Zero Trust, IPv6 — modern networking concepts on the exam.

encounters.question: What is the core principle of Zero Trust security?
options: Trust all internal network traffic by default
Trust external users after multi-factor authentication
Never trust, always verify — no implicit trust based on network location
Trust verified users indefinitely within a session
encounters.explanation: Zero Trust assumes breach: verify every user, device, and connection explicitly. Internal network location confers no implicit trust. Access is granted per-session with least-privilege.

encounters.question: How long is an IPv6 address?
encounters.explanation: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits (vs IPv4's 32 bits), written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits. This provides 340 undecillion addresses — effectively unlimited.

encounters.question: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
encounters.explanation: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback (equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4). FE80::/10 is link-local, FF02::1 is all-nodes multicast.

encounters.question: IPv6 link-local addresses use which prefix?
encounters.explanation: IPv6 link-local addresses (FE80::/10) are automatically configured on all IPv6 interfaces and are only valid on the local link — they cannot be routed.

encounters.question: What does SDN (Software-Defined Networking) separate?
options: The control plane (routing logic) from the data plane (packet forwarding)
encounters.explanation: SDN decouples the control plane (routing decisions, managed by a central controller) from the data plane (actual packet forwarding on switches). This enables programmable network management.

encounters.question: SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) combines which two categories of technology?
options: SD-WAN and cloud-delivered network security services (CASB, SWG, ZTNA)
MDM and endpoint detection and response (EDR)
encounters.explanation: SASE (coined by Gartner) merges SD-WAN with cloud security services (Secure Web Gateway, CASB, Zero Trust Network Access, FWaaS) delivered as a single cloud service.

encounters.question: VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) is used to:
options: Encrypt all traffic on a VLAN segment
Extend Layer 2 network segments over a Layer 3 IP network
Replace VLANs entirely in campus networks
Provide wireless QoS for voice traffic
encounters.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates Layer 2 Ethernet frames in UDP packets, allowing Layer 2 segments to span across Layer 3 networks. It supports 16 million virtual networks (vs VLAN's 4094 limit).

encounters.question: What is micro-segmentation in a Zero Trust architecture?
options: Using VLANs smaller than /28 for network segments
Dividing the network into small isolated zones with granular per-workload access controls
Implementing QoS policies at the packet level
Splitting physical switches into multiple virtual switches
encounters.explanation: Micro-segmentation applies fine-grained security policies at the workload level (e.g., individual VMs or containers), preventing lateral movement even within the data center.

encounters.question: IPv6 uses which mechanism instead of ARP for address resolution?
encounters.explanation: IPv6 replaces ARP with NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol), which uses ICMPv6 messages. NDP handles address resolution, router discovery, and duplicate address detection.

encounters.question: SD-WAN primarily improves upon traditional WAN in which way?
options: By replacing MPLS with IPSec tunnels exclusively
By intelligently routing traffic across multiple connection types (MPLS, broadband, LTE) based on real-time performance
By eliminating the need for any encryption on WAN links
By forcing all traffic through a central data center for inspection
encounters.explanation: SD-WAN dynamically routes traffic across multiple WAN links (MPLS, cable, LTE) based on real-time metrics (latency, jitter, loss), optimizing cost and performance. It does NOT mandate IPSec-only.

guardian_encounters.question: Which OSI layer adds IP source and destination addresses to a segment?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) adds the IP header. Layer 4 adds port numbers, Layer 2 adds MAC addresses.

guardian_encounters.question: What port does HTTPS use?
guardian_encounters.explanation: HTTPS uses port 443. HTTP uses port 80.

guardian_encounters.question: A switch forwards traffic based on what?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Switches use MAC address tables (CAM tables) to make Layer 2 forwarding decisions.

guardian_encounters.question: How many usable host addresses are in a /26 subnet?
guardian_encounters.explanation: /26 = 64 total (2^6) minus 2 = 62 usable hosts.

guardian_encounters.question: IaaS is best described as:
options: A managed runtime for developers (App Engine)
Raw compute, storage, and networking infrastructure (EC2, Azure VMs)
guardian_encounters.explanation: IaaS = raw infrastructure. PaaS = developer platform. SaaS = software applications. NFV = virtualized network functions.

guardian_encounters.question: Single-mode fiber vs multi-mode fiber — which supports the longer distance?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Single-mode uses a laser and a narrow core, supporting distances of 10km to 100km+. Multi-mode uses LED/VCSEL and supports up to ~550m.

guardian_encounters.question: Zero Trust security is based on which principle?
options: Trust but verify all internal traffic
Never trust, always verify regardless of network location
guardian_encounters.explanation: Zero Trust: never implicitly trust any user or device. Every access request is verified, regardless of whether it comes from inside or outside the network perimeter.

guardian_encounters.question: SSH uses which port?
guardian_encounters.explanation: SSH = port 22. FTP = 21. Telnet = 23. HTTPS = 443.

guardian_encounters.question: In spine-and-leaf architecture, any two leaf switches communicate in how many hops?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Spine-and-leaf guarantees leaf→spine→leaf = exactly 2 hops for any server-to-server communication, providing consistent and predictable latency.

guardian_encounters.question: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
guardian_encounters.explanation: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback. 127.0.0.1 is IPv4 loopback. FE80::1 is a link-local address.

guardian_encounters.question: DHCP uses which ports?
guardian_encounters.explanation: DHCP server = UDP 67, client = UDP 68. DNS = 53. TFTP = 69. SNMP = 161/162.

guardian_encounters.question: An IPS differs from an IDS in that an IPS:
options: Sits inline and actively blocks detected threats
Requires manual intervention to respond to threats
guardian_encounters.explanation: IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is inline and blocks threats in real time. IDS (Intrusion Detection System) is passive — it detects and alerts but doesn't block.

guardian_encounters.question: What RFC 1918 private address range corresponds to /12 (172.16.0.0/12)?
guardian_encounters.explanation: 172.16.0.0/12 covers 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255. Addresses starting with 172.32 and above are PUBLIC. This is a common exam trap.

guardian_encounters.question: SDN separates which two planes?
guardian_encounters.explanation: SDN separates the control plane (routing/logic decisions) from the data plane (actual packet forwarding). The control plane moves to a centralized controller.

guardian_encounters.question: Host A (192.168.1.50/26) sends a packet to 192.168.1.100. What happens?
options: Sent to the default gateway — different subnets
Sent to the DNS server for resolution first
guardian_encounters.explanation: /26 = 64 addresses per subnet. 192.168.1.0/26 covers .0-.63; 192.168.1.64/26 covers .64-.127. Host .50 is in subnet .0/26; host .100 is in subnet .64/26. Different subnets → traffic goes to the default gateway.

guardian_encounters.question: What is APIPA and when does a host use it?
options: 169.254.0.0/16 — assigned automatically when a DHCP server is unreachable
192.168.0.0/16 — default range assigned by home routers
guardian_encounters.explanation: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) assigns 169.254.x.x when DHCP fails. The host can only communicate with others on the same APIPA range — it has no gateway and no DNS.

guardian_encounters.question: Cat6a supports 10 Gbps up to what distance?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Cat6a (Augmented Cat6) supports 10GBase-T at the full 100-meter distance. Standard Cat6 is limited to 55m at 10 Gbps.

guardian_encounters.question: SNMP traps are sent to the manager on which port?
guardian_encounters.explanation: SNMP manager polls agents on port 161. Agents send unsolicited TRAP messages to the manager on port 162. Syslog uses 514.

guardian_encounters.question: IPv6 replaces ARP with which protocol?
guardian_encounters.explanation: IPv6 uses NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) over ICMPv6 for address resolution, router discovery, and duplicate address detection — replacing ARP entirely.

guardian_encounters.question: A UTM appliance consolidates which set of functions?
options: DHCP, DNS, NTP, and RADIUS in one box
Firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, web filtering, and VPN in one device
guardian_encounters.explanation: UTM (Unified Threat Management) integrates multiple security functions — stateful firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, web content filter, and VPN — into a single appliance.
